summary: Broaden estimation practice with a geometric sense check and a compact set of reusable scale anchors.

improvements.why: The note checks whether a final value sounds sensible but does not show how to test a volume estimate against a familiar object's size; ER 9702 w20 P13 Q1 recommends taking cube roots for a football-volume item.
improvements.what: Add a short inverse sense check: for a roughly cubic or spherical object, take the cube root of a proposed volume to recover a characteristic length, then compare it with the object's known size. Use the football options as a paraphrased example without copying the question.

improvements.why: The bank has many forward estimates but no question asking the learner to reject an implausible volume by recovering a length scale; the learner's question guide also practices estimates in a quantity, unit and order-of-magnitude table.
improvements.what: One generated Identify MCQ comparing proposed everyday-object volumes by cube-root size, one Suggest short item asking how to check an unfamiliar volume estimate, and one structured table item estimating the order of magnitude and unit for a car mass, paper thickness or time between heartbeats. Include explanations and three progressive hints; use only bundle command words.

improvements.why: The learner's revision guide gives useful cross-topic scale anchors beyond the note's adult, sprinter and atom examples; Cambridge outcome 9702-1.1.2 asks for reasonable estimates across quantities in the syllabus.
improvements.source: library: sources/library/SaveMyExams/9702 a-level-physics-cie-25/9702 c1.1.pdf p.3; sources/library/SaveMyExams/TQ 9702 a-level-physics-cie-25-questions-only/TQ 9702 c1.1.pdf pp.18-19 | https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664565-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf
improvements.what: Add a compact, paraphrased anchor table with a few distinct quantities such as car mass about $10^3\ \mathrm{kg}$, speed of sound in air about $3\times10^2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and atmospheric pressure about $10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$; show that these are approximate checks, not exact data.
